images.caption:
Inside "Hezekiah's tunnel," the 8th century water channel cut through bedrock right under the City of David. The channel brought water from the Gihon spring (on the north-eastern slope of the hill) to the Siloam pool at the southern tip of the city. King Hezekiah ordered construction of this water system to secure a water source inside the city walls in the face of the approaching Assyrian army. When the channel was finished, the entrance to the spring was covered over with rubble to prevent the Assyrians from using (or tampering with) the water.

Jerusalem

images.caption: The Al-Aqsa Mosque (also spelled El-Aksa; "Distant Mosque") is the most important mosque in Jerusalem. Located on the Haram esh-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary) or Temple Mount, it is the third holiest site in Islam after Mecca and Medina. It is the central focus of the Muslim community in Jerusalem, hosting daily prayers and accommodating large crowds for Friday sermons.
images.alt: The Al-Aqsa Mosque (also spelled El-Aksa; "Distant Mosque") is the most important mosque in Jerusalem. images.caption: This photograph shows a modern replica of the Arch of Titus relief depicting the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple, including the temple menorah, carried in a triumphal procession through Rome following the Roman conquest of Jerusalem in 70 CE. The replica was created for the ANU – Museum of the Jewish People in Tel Aviv as part of its permanent exhibition (ID #178505). It reproduces the section of the original marble relief sculpted on the inner south panel of the Arch of Titus in Rome (c. 81 CE), commissioned by Emperor Domitian to commemorate his brother Titus's victory in the First Jewish–Roman War.
